title: Catching Mutagens on a Bacterial Plate
endLine: Revertants above background flag bacterial mutagens, not human cancer risk.

scenes.tts: Animal cancer studies take years. How can bacteria on a dish screen a chemical for DNA mutation in a few days? Bruce Ames turned broken Salmonella into living detectors.
scenes.caption: Animal cancer studies take years. How can bacteria on a dish screen a chemical for DNA mutation in a few days? Bruce Ames turned broken Salmonella into living detectors.
scenes.visual: Top-down lab bench view centered on a petri dish of Salmonella beside a pipette holding a test chemical droplet (schematic; no molecular structures). A schematic calendar flips past years and fades out while the dish enlarges to fill most of the frame height under a bold question mark; bright colonies begin glowing on the agar as Bruce Ames is named.
scenes.narration: Animal cancer studies take years. How can bacteria on a dish screen a chemical for DNA mutation in a few days? Bruce Ames turned broken Salmonella into living detectors.

scenes.visual: The same bench petri dish remains centered with gentle ambient shimmer while the title 'Catching Mutagens on a Bacterial Plate' appears cleanly above it in large high-contrast text, then fades out.

scenes.tts: The test uses Salmonella strains that cannot make the amino acid histidine. On a dish with trace histidine, cells divide a few times and stop. Only a new mutation restoring histidine synthesis lets a cell form a colony. Each colony is a revertant, marking one such mutation. Untreated dishes also grow a few revertants: the spontaneous background.
scenes.caption: The test uses Salmonella strains that cannot make the amino acid histidine. On a dish with trace histidine, cells divide a few times and stop. Only a new mutation restoring histidine synthesis lets a cell form a colony. Each colony is a revertant, marking one such mutation. Untreated dishes also grow a few revertants: the spontaneous background.
scenes.visual: Same petri dish zoomed in (schematic). A small side gauge labeled 'trace histidine' empties as schematic bacterial specks divide a few times and stall into a faint background haze. One cell flashes a bright mutation pulse, keeps dividing after the gauge hits zero, and grows into a prominent bright colony labeled 'revertant'. A few scattered colonies on a matching untreated dish are labeled 'background' (schematic).
scenes.narration: The test uses Salmonella strains that cannot make the amino acid histidine. On a dish with trace histidine, cells divide a few times and stop. Only a new mutation restoring histidine synthesis lets a cell form a colony. Each colony is a revertant, marking one such mutation. Untreated dishes also grow a few revertants: the spontaneous background.

scenes.tts: Outside agents that cause mutations are mutagens, and different mutagens change DNA differently. So the test uses separate strains. T A one hundred reverts mainly by base-pair substitution, swapping one base pair for another. T A ninety-eight reverts mainly by frameshift, adding or removing bases not in multiples of three.
scenes.caption: Outside agents that cause mutations are mutagens, and different mutagens change DNA differently. So the test uses separate strains. TA100 reverts mainly by base-pair substitution, swapping one base pair for another. TA98 reverts mainly by frameshift, adding or removing bases not in multiples of three.
scenes.visual: The single bench dish smoothly divides into two side-by-side dishes labeled 'TA100' and 'TA98' (schematic; no molecular structures). Below TA100, a schematic DNA ladder swaps one colored rung for another ('base-pair swap'). Below TA98, a schematic ladder drops one rung so downstream three-base brackets shift out of register ('frameshift').
scenes.narration: Outside agents that cause mutations are mutagens, and different mutagens change DNA differently. So the test uses separate strains. TA100 reverts mainly by base-pair substitution, swapping one base pair for another. TA98 reverts mainly by frameshift, adding or removing bases not in multiples of three.

scenes.tts: Yet many carcinogens do nothing to bacteria alone. Benzo a pyrene binds DNA only after liver enzymes oxidize it into reactive products. So dishes run with and without S nine, a rat-liver enzyme fraction. A rising revertant count with liver enzymes flags a bacterial mutagen, not human cancer.
scenes.caption: Yet many carcinogens do nothing to bacteria alone. Benzo[a]pyrene binds DNA only after liver enzymes oxidize it into reactive products. So dishes run with and without S9, a rat-liver enzyme fraction. A rising revertant count with liver enzymes flags a bacterial mutagen, not human cancer.
scenes.visual: Same bench layout with two paired dishes: '-S9' and '+S9' (schematic; no molecular structures). A pale chemical token labeled 'benzo[a]pyrene' drops onto the -S9 dish with no colony rise. A vial labeled 'S9 liver enzymes' mixes with the token before dropping onto the +S9 dish; the token turns bright orange and new revertant colonies bloom across the plate.
scenes.narration: Yet many carcinogens do nothing to bacteria alone. Benzo[a]pyrene binds DNA only after liver enzymes oxidize it into reactive products. So dishes run with and without S9, a rat-liver enzyme fraction. A rising revertant count with liver enzymes flags a bacterial mutagen, not human cancer.

scenes.tts: Test Compound X at three rising doses. Background is about one hundred twenty in T A one hundred, thirty in T A ninety-eight. Without S nine, T A one hundred stays flat; so does T A ninety-eight with S nine. Only T A one hundred with S nine climbs: two hundred forty, four hundred eighty, nine hundred fifty. What does X do?
scenes.caption: Test Compound X at three rising doses. Background is about 120 in TA100, 30 in TA98. Without S9, TA100 stays flat; so does TA98 with S9. Only TA100 with S9 climbs: 240, 480, 950. What does X do?
scenes.visual: Beside the paired dishes on the bench, a computed bar chart builds directly from the plate counts (exact lesson numbers, not schematic): baseline dashes at 120 (TA100) and 30 (TA98); flat bars for TA100 -S9 (125, 118, 130) and TA98 +S9 (30, 28, 35); and three sharply rising bars for TA100 +S9 (240, 480, 950). The question 'What does Compound X do?' appears prominently above the bars.
scenes.narration: Test Compound X at three rising doses. Background is about 120 in TA100, 30 in TA98. Without S9, TA100 stays flat; so does TA98 with S9. Only TA100 with S9 climbs: 240, 480, 950. What does X do?

scenes.visual: The computed bar chart for Compound X and the question 'What does Compound X do?' remain clearly visible on the bench while a gentle 4.5-second circular timer ticks quietly in the corner.

scenes.tts: Divide each count by background. Two hundred forty over one hundred twenty is two. Four hundred eighty is four, and nine hundred fifty is about eight. The rise needs liver enzymes, so a metabolite acts; X itself shows no detectable effect. T A one hundred reverts by base-pair substitution, so that metabolite causes base-pair substitutions in Salmonella.
scenes.caption: Divide each count by background. 240 over 120 is 2. 480 is 4, and 950 is about 8. The rise needs liver enzymes, so a metabolite acts; X itself shows no detectable effect. TA100 reverts by base-pair substitution, so that metabolite causes base-pair substitutions in Salmonella.
scenes.visual: On the same computed bar chart, the formula 'count / background' appears at top. As each ratio is spoken, '240 / 120 = 2x', '480 / 120 = 4x', and '950 / 120 ≈ 8x' illuminate in sequence above the three TA100 +S9 bars. The TA100 dish and S9 vial glow together with the label 'metabolite -> base-pair substitutions' (schematic).
scenes.narration: Divide each count by background. 240 over 120 is 2. 480 is 4, and 950 is about 8. The rise needs liver enzymes, so a metabolite acts; X itself shows no detectable effect. TA100 reverts by base-pair substitution, so that metabolite causes base-pair substitutions in Salmonella.

scenes.tts: Always check four things in order: background, dose response, strains, and S nine. A positive shows bacterial mutation, not cancer risk in people. A negative never proves safety either. Some carcinogens act without mutating DNA, or through processes bacteria lack.
scenes.caption: Always check four things in order: background, dose response, strains, and S9. A positive shows bacterial mutation, not cancer risk in people. A negative never proves safety either. Some carcinogens act without mutating DNA, or through processes bacteria lack.
scenes.visual: Four numbered highlight markers sweep across the bench chart in order: '1 background', '2 dose', '3 strains', '4 ±S9'. The bench then splits cleanly into two guardrail panels (schematic): a crowded revertant dish paired with 'mutates bacteria' and a crossed-out arrow to 'human cancer'; an empty dish paired with a crossed-out 'safe' badge and 'non-mutagenic routes'.
scenes.narration: Always check four things in order: background, dose response, strains, and S9. A positive shows bacterial mutation, not cancer risk in people. A negative never proves safety either. Some carcinogens act without mutating DNA, or through processes bacteria lack.

scenes.tts: Once liver extract joined the dish, discoveries followed. In 1973, Ames and colleagues showed liver extract turned eighteen tested carcinogens into frameshift mutagens. In 1975, Joyce McCann and colleagues found one hundred fifty-six of one hundred seventy-four carcinogens in their tested set mutagenic.
scenes.caption: Once liver extract joined the dish, discoveries followed. In 1973, Ames and colleagues showed liver extract turned 18 tested carcinogens into frameshift mutagens. In 1975, Joyce McCann and colleagues found 156 of 174 carcinogens in their tested set mutagenic.
scenes.visual: The petri dish and S9 vial anchor the left side of the bench while two crisp results animate on the right: first '1973 · Ames et al. · 18 carcinogens -> frameshifts' (schematic dish pulse), then a computed proportion bar '1975 · McCann et al. · 156 of 174 in tested set' filling to 156/174.
scenes.narration: Once liver extract joined the dish, discoveries followed. In 1973, Ames and colleagues showed liver extract turned 18 tested carcinogens into frameshift mutagens. In 1975, Joyce McCann and colleagues found 156 of 174 carcinogens in their tested set mutagenic.

scenes.tts: The assay soon tested everyday products. In 1975, Ames, Kammen, and Yamasaki found one hundred fifty of one hundred sixty-nine hair-dye formulations mutagenic. In 1978, Barry Commoner and colleagues found mutagens in cooked ground beef. Each dish flags bacterial mutation, while human cancer risk needs other evidence.
scenes.caption: The assay soon tested everyday products. In 1975, Ames, Kammen, and Yamasaki found 150 of 169 hair-dye formulations mutagenic. In 1978, Barry Commoner and colleagues found mutagens in cooked ground beef. Each dish flags bacterial mutation, while human cancer risk needs other evidence.
scenes.visual: Continuing on the same bench, two new cards slide in beside the dish (schematic icons, no molecular structures): a dye bottle paired with a computed proportion bar filling to 150/169 ('1975 · 150 of 169 hair dyes'), followed by a skillet icon ('1978 · Commoner et al. · cooked ground beef'). The petri dish glows once more at center beside 'bacterial mutation ≠ human cancer'.
scenes.narration: The assay soon tested everyday products. In 1975, Ames, Kammen, and Yamasaki found 150 of 169 hair-dye formulations mutagenic. In 1978, Barry Commoner and colleagues found mutagens in cooked ground beef. Each dish flags bacterial mutation, while human cancer risk needs other evidence.
